summary: Zelus, also spelled Zelos (Ancient Greek: Ζῆλος), is a daimon in Greek mythology who personifies dedication, emulation, eager rivalry, envy, and zeal. He is one of the four winged enforcers in the retinue of Zeus, alongside his siblings Nike, Kratos, and Bia. The modern English word "zeal" derives from his name, and his Roman counterpart was Invidia.
etymology: From Ancient Greek Ζῆλος (Zēlos), meaning "zeal," "emulation," or "eager rivalry"; the English word "zeal" derives from it.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Zelus is the son of the Titan Pallas and the Oceanid Styx. His siblings are Nike (Victory), Kratos (Strength), and Bia (Force), with whom he is closely associated as a group of personified abstractions that attend the king of the gods.
The four siblings are consistently named together in ancient sources as the embodiment of qualities that serve and uphold the authority of Zeus.

sections.heading: Mythology
paragraphs: According to Hesiod's Theogony, Zelus and his siblings dwell always in the presence of Zeus and follow wherever he leads. When Zeus summoned the gods to Mount Olympus to wage war against the Titans, Styx was the first to come, bringing her children to his side.

In gratitude for this allegiance during the Titanomachy, Zeus honored Styx and her offspring, granting them permanent places at his side and appointing Styx herself to be the great oath of the gods. Zelus thus functions as a winged enforcer in Zeus's retinue, embodying the competitive zeal and emulation that sustain the divine order.

sections.heading: Character and reception
paragraphs: Beyond his role as a servant of Zeus, Zelus is also associated with the darker side of rivalry. In Hesiod's Works and Days, the figure named Zelus (rendered as "Envy") is described as foul-mouthed and delighting in evil, a force tied to the strife of the Iron Age.

His Roman equivalent was Invidia, whose name carries the sense of looking upon another with hostility, and the figure was later linked to the concept of envy among the deadly sins. In some later traditions the personification was recast to emphasize religious fervor or zeal.
